articles.title: THE CURRENT OF THE SPIRIT
articles.author: W. Dickson
articles.meeting: Word in meeting for ministry, St

paragraphs.text: On Lord’s day reference was made to the verse in Psalm 46, “There is a river the streams whereof make glad the city of God”. In its application to us, that passage suggests that there is a current flowing connected with the presence of the Spirit of God here. Now it is always an exercise as to whether we are moving with the Spirit in that current. Reference was also made to the river in Ezekiel 47. In that remarkable scripture it says (Ezekiel 47: 11) that the marshes and the pools shall not be healed but be given up to salt. This would be a solemn reminder to us of the danger of stagnation through failing to keep in the current of the Spirit’s activities and movements.

I thought that these scriptures in the Acts would set out the great current of the Spirit’s activities identified with the apostles and culminating in the service of Paul, and would have a current application to us. It is interesting that when Saul of Tarsus was converted Ananias failed for a moment—without in any sense casting a reflection on him—to get into the divine current. He demurred at the message received from the Lord to go and seek out Saul. He was not aware sensibly at that moment of the current that was flowing. Then a little later even Peter had to be adjusted in regard to the current of the Spirit towards the gentiles.

Now the scriptures we have read all show a remarkable ability on the part of persons to be in the current of the Spirit. We dwell sometimes on the failure of Barnabas with regard to John Mark, but it is good to think of the very interesting side of his character which comes out in Acts 11. The Lord’s hand was with certain gentiles and a great number of Greeks “believed and turned to the Lord. And the report concerning them reached the ears of the assembly which was in Jerusalem, and they sent out Barnabas to go through as far as Antioch—who, having arrived and seeing the grace of God, rejoiced and exhorted all with purpose of heart to abide with the Lord; for he was a good man and full of the Holy Spirit and of faith; and a large crowd of people were added to the Lord. And he went away to Tarsus to seek out Saul”. How beautifully Barnabas moved in relation to the current that was flowing at that time. You would have thought that Saul would have been very well known in Tarsus, but it says that Barnabas had to seek him out. Then it says, “and having found him”. What diligence marked Barnabas, nor was there any slackening of this diligence because Saul might displace him. However, as helped by the Spirit of God to see the character of the current that was flowing at that time. Barnabas’s service resulted in this great matter of the assembly at Antioch. There was a freshness about the assembly in Antioch which was quite different from Jerusalem, as it was set up without a trace of the Judaising features which hampered and restricted even the apostles at Jerusalem. Barnabas, as in the Spirit’s current, was used to bring forward Saul of Tarsus to help this beautiful assembly.
This current was still flowing in chapter 16. This remarkable current has flowed westward right to these islands and to the place where we are at

this time. Paul and his company “immediately … sought to go forth to Macedonia”. Then it says, “we went in a straight course to Samothracia”, as if they had immediately, without hesitation, linked themselves on with the current. Once they had received such clarity of direction from the Spirit of God in the call from the Macedonian man, they immediately put themselves into the current of divine activity which resulted in the bringing to light of this fine assembly at Philippi. That current was flowing locally too, as seen in the praying women by the riverside, and this was to develop into everything that was choice in regard to the great thought of the assembly.

In Acts 18, although Apollos was an eloquent man and mighty in the Scriptures, he was not fully in the current. However, Aquila and Priscilla were available to help him. What a practical word that is as to whether every brother and sister, every husband and wife in our localities are so in the current of divine activities themselves that they can take a brother like Apollos and unfold to him “the way of God more exactly”.

These three choice instances show the undeviating movements of the Spirit (which continue to the present time) and that there were persons available to link themselves on with the Spirit to further and strengthen the work of God in the places where they were. The localities are specially mentioned—Antioch, Philippi, Ephesus. Well, we all of us have to ask ourselves whether we are in the current, or whether we are stagnant. Can we discern the movements of the Spirit of God and the way He is flowing at the present time? Is any ministry I give locally or generally, or any work I do in my locality, linked with the current that is flowing? Is any interest I have in the

truth related to the current? Do my thoughts for any persons I am interested in relate to the current that is flowing? These are very practical matters, because the enemy would try to divert us from the current. He would suggest that, because of the calamities and breakdown which have come in, there is a lack of direction for the christian. But that is not the case, as we can be in the current of the Spirit in relation to each of our local assemblies. The question would be whether we are among those who readily discern the flow of the current and further it by our activities in our local places. In each of these three places the work of God came to light in relation to persons who recognised the current of the Spirit. So that is the word for us in every one of our localities, and for every person in them, to test ourselves as to whether we are in the current of the Spirit at the present time. May we all be so, for His name’s sake.

In the second scripture Paul speaks of Timotheus as putting the Corinthians in mind of his ways “as they are in Christ”. He says, “according as I teach everywhere in every assembly”. In Acts 20 we have set out for us by the beloved apostle himself his ways as they were in Christ.

In the third scripture we have the reference to his teaching and conduct, the two thoughts going together, as they do in Acts 20. Paul had reminded the Ephesian elders that he had not shrunk from announcing to them all the counsel of God. He had these great and glorious matters in his heart, the glad tidings of the grace of God, the preaching of the kingdom of God, and then all the counsel of God. But there was something additional to that—his ways as they were in Christ. He reminds them of how he had been among them, saying, “I have showed you all things”. The note says, Specially, ‘to show by example’. He also says, “Wherefore watch, remembering that for three years, night and day, I ceased not admonishing each one of you with tears”. He is speaking to the overseers, and I believe the Lord would exercise us, even those of us who are younger, as to the matter of being overseers as caring unofficially for the things of God. As we think of the assembly of God that He has purchased with the blood of His own, I think we would be encouraged to have our part in caring, according to our measure, for divine things.

In 1 Timothy 3 Paul raised the question of qualification for caring for the assembly of God, which, of course, is a challenging matter, an exercising matter, because clearly the Lord needs persons who can care for assembly interests down here. So Paul says, “Take heed therefore to yourselves, and to all the flock, wherein the Holy Spirit has set you as overseers, to shepherd the assembly of God”. What a shepherd he had been—how he took character from his Master! His desire now was that others should shepherd the assembly of God of which he speaks in this affecting way, “the assembly of God, which he has purchased with the blood of his own”. How God values His assembly! It is a word that would appeal to our affections, “The blood of his own”, His own Son, His own Lamb, involved in the purchase of the assembly of God. We are in a broken day, which the last scripture has in mind, and I believe the Lord would encourage us all to fill out our part in this matter of shepherd care, shepherding the assembly of God. If we are to have any part in that, I think we need to see the character of what was set on by Paul. “I have shewed you all things, that thus labouring we ought to come in aid of the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said. It is more blessed to give than to receive”.

How Paul served! You think of how the Samaritan served, the loneliness involved, the insignificant title used as to him, “a certain Samaritan” (Luke 10: 33), over against all that was official, all that was of the lawyer character. Well, Paul says, “Remember the words of the Lord Jesus”. As has often been said, you do not exactly find these words in Scripture, but clearly they are written on the pages of the gospels, “the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, It is more blessed to give than to receive”. So Paul served in the spirit of self-sacrificing love. Think of the Samaritan putting the man on his own beast. Apart from any typical application, the man was prepared in self-sacrificing love to serve that soul for his restoration and good. So Paul here is prepared in self-sacrificing love to serve the saints, “Remembering that for three years, night and day, I ceased not admonishing each of of you with tears”.

One hesitates in speaking of a chapter like this because of the glory of it, the glory of Paul’s ways as they were in Christ. It makes one feel so small and puny in relation to one’s affections and preparedness to sacrifice for God and for

Christ to think of the stature of Paul the beloved apostle, and to think of how his affections had been formed by the blessed God and by the Holy Spirit. His affections had been formed so that he could care for the saints in this attractive manner. He was not narrow in his affections, not self-centred. He was broad in his affections as shown when he speaks of the Ephesians having love to all the saints. How much love the apostle had for all the saints, bearing the burdens of all the assemblies. Then he says, “Who is weak, and I am not weak?”, 2 Corinthians 11: 29. Think of the beloved apostle caring for every saint. How near he was to Christ; how near he was to the Master! We can think about these things, however small our formation in love may be. My formation in love is very small, yet one can look at the beloved apostle, a man of like passions with ourselves, and see how he was formed in the divine nature and how his affections moved him in self-sacrificing service to the saints. We can think of him, as he says to the Corinthians, as a model, “I entreat you therefore, be my imitators”. I might be like a Corinthian, a party man, or just carnal, a babe in Christ with no formation spiritually, no formation in the divine nature, yet Paul would say, “I entreat you therefore, be my imitators”. He says, “For if ye should have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet not many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the glad tidings”.

Paul was not only a shepherd but a father, and he handed these things on to Timothy. His fervent desire was that Timothy should entrust things to faithful men. That is the way things have come down to us. Not only the teaching, but the ways in Christ, the conduct, are handed down on that line: these things “entrust to faithful men, such as shall be competent to instruct others also”,

2 Timothy 2; 2. So Timothy had learned Paul’s ways as they were in Christ. What skill Paul used, what skill as a shepherd, what skill as a father, and Timothy was like him. “For this reason I have sent to you Timotheus, who is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, who shall put you in mind of my ways as they are in Christ, according as I teach everywhere in every assembly”. So he sent a comparatively young man to Corinth where there was great need of fatherhood. I do not think the apostle would use these words if he did not really feel there was great need of fatherhood in Corinth, “Not as chiding do I write these things to you, but as my beloved children I admonish you”. In spite of conditions in Corinth he writes thus to them, his affections are so great.

I feel sometimes that when a problem arises amongst us the lawyer mind comes up. Of course, we should, and must, cling to divine principles, but then there is this other side of Paul’s ways in Christ, shown in how he cared for these Corinthians because they were his beloved children. “I write these things to you ... as my beloved children I admonish you”. He loved them; he was not going to part with them easily. In his skill, with the help of the Spirit of God, and in wisdom, he was used of the Lord to bring them round; even the one who had to be withdrawn from was recovered. One hesitates to speak of these things because of the stature of the man; he was so near to Christ. The Lord says, “As to those whom thou hast given me, I have not lost one of them”, John 18: 9. He had kept them think of how He loved them! The Lord set out this parental thought of care for His own. Then Paul set it out, and now he has a child who is like him, “For this reason I have sent to you Timotheus, who is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord”. It has often been remarked that he did not send Titus;

he sent Timotheus. Timotheus would be tender in spite of the conditions. It is “in the Lord”, of course, but there would be the spirit of fatherly care in Timotheus in Corinth, “who shall put you in mind of my ways as they are in Christ”—these ways are not in Adam; they are not in the flesh; his ways were in Christ. We cannot work up to them in any human way, it must be as we are near to the Father and to the Lord Jesus, and as we are formed by the Holy Spirit that we can have any part in shepherd care or in fatherhood as set out in Paul. I think that as we cultivate links with divine Persons that then we shall develop in features of shepherd care and fatherhood.

So in the last scripture Paul says to Timothy, “Thou hast been thoroughly acquainted with my teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, longsuffering, love, endurance, persecutions, sufferings”. So, as in Acts 20, it is not just the teaching. Teaching is first, and how important it is. Paul says, “Every scripture is divinely inspired, and profitable for teaching, for conviction, for correction, for instruction in righteousness”. Who would want in any sense to set aside right teaching? It is fundamental. But then as well as teaching there is “conduct, purpose, faith ...”. So what a man Paul was; how he had been formed in the knowledge of God, formed through suffering, so that his conduct set out his ways in Christ. Really, Christ was being set out in Paul; it is the “way of more surpassing excellence”, 1 Corinthians 12: 31. Now he is passing all this on to Timothy, against a background of departure, and difficult times. He lets him know that “in the last days difficult times shall be there; for men shall be lovers of self” (2 Timothy 3: 1, 2). There is no care of the saints in that. “Lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, evil speakers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful”. Then Paul says

specifically, “But thou hast been thoroughly acquainted with my teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, longsuffering, love”—not half acquainted, but thoroughly acquainted. In contrast we have all the other features of the last days, “Lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God” (2 Timothy 3: 4)—men’s hearts gone off into idolatry, far from God, not having been secured by the glad tidings to love Him.

Over against this we have a man not only understanding the teaching but understanding the conduct that was appropriate to the teaching. As someone said recently, it is not only to talk about the truth, but to walk in the truth. That is what Paul did, and Timothy had been thoroughly acquainted with both his teaching and his conduct. So Paul goes on, “But thou, abide in those things which thou hast learned, and of which thou hast been fully persuaded, knowing of whom thou hast learned them”. He had learned them from Paul, and Paul had learned them from Christ. We have no hesitation in saying that. If we speak as to our on day we would not speak of a Paul now; there has been only one Paul. But Paul was an imitator of Christ. Timothy learned the teaching and the conduct from Paul—“Knowing of whom thou hast learned then; and that from a child thou hast known the sacred letters”. So we would encourage the children. Get to know the Scriptures while you are young. They are “able to make thee wise unto salvation, through faith which is in Christ Jesus. Every scripture is divinely inspired, and profitable for teaching, for conviction, for correction, for instruction in righteousness”. So all this has in mind the matter of care. The saints are to be cared for. They need all these things. If I am to have any power in caring for them I must know the Scriptures. So how important it is that there should be the reading of the Scriptures in the household, and by the children themselves, in view of
our being formed and taught so as to care for God’s interests in days of difficulty.

Now I just mention in closing a word in the next chapter. Paul says, “Alexander the smith did many evil things against me. The Lord will render to him according to his works. Against whom be thou also on thy guard, for he has greatly withstood our words” (2 Timothy 4: 14, 15). It is just that word “guard” that is in mind. That is another feature of care, guarding. There are certain historical matters, such as this, that Paul does not forget. Paul is not rendering it to Alexander; he says that the Lord will render to him according to his works. Well, this is a feature of care. What Paul is handing down to Timothy is not only the positive side of care, of helping souls, but also this feature of guarding, which we must not overlook. This man had been an opposer; he did many evil things against Paul. These are things that we may need to remember. Certain persons have been withdrawn from, and rightly withdrawn from, who may have had a history in what was wrong. We just have to be on our guard, particularly with leaders, without setting aside the spirit of the dispensation, or the Lord’s sovereign rights in recovery. Paul says, “The Lord will render to him”. I do not think it alters Paul’s spirit at all, but there is just this word of warning. There had been a course in what was wrong in this man Alexander and there was the need to be on guard. So this is a feature of care that Paul passes on to Timotheus, and he would, in turn, hand it down to us; that is the way that things have come down to us these things “ entrust to faithful men, such as shall be competent to instruct others also” (2 Timothy 2: 2). We are to come into the “others also”. So there is this feature of guarding what is due to the Lord, guarding the rights of the Lord. There have been assembly judgments that God has honoured and we need
to respect them. We need to guard what is pleasing to God and to the rights of the Lord.

May we be encouraged by these thoughts. Unless we are near to God, unless we are formed in the divine nature, I do not think we can have any part in the care of divine interests, but I believe God would encourage us. The Lord Jesus is available, and what an example He has given—“He Himself said, It is more blessed to give than to receive”. Let it move us in this line of self-sacrificing love in the care of the saints, which the Lord Jesus Himself has set on—“ … our Lord Jesus Christ … for your sakes he, being rich, became poor, in order that ye by his poverty might be enriched”, 2 Corinthians 8: 9. It was self-sacrificing love in view of the care of the saints. Paul set it out in his ways in Christ and he passed it on to Timothy. Timothy displayed it and he passes it on to “faithful men, such as shall be competent to instruct others also”. May we come in there, beloved brethren, in this administration of divine care and supply. And then there is just this thought of guarding which we must remember, else we shall lose what the Lord has preserved amongst us in its preciousness. It does not mean that our spirits are to be harsh toward anyone, but we should be careful and we should respect assembly judgments. May the Lord bless the word.

articles.title: SELF-WILL SHOULD NOT RESIST THE PROPHETIC WORD
articles.author: B. Taylor
articles.place: Word in meeting for ministry, Brooklyn, N.Y.

paragraphs.text: Our brother prayed that self will may not interfere with the flow of the prophetic word. That challenged me, as I am sure it would challenge all of us—whether there might be any self-will with us that would interfere at this time. In the verses read, self-will interfered with the progress of the kingdom, but the word of God met it. Saul had turned away from following, from paying attention and hearkening to the word of Jehovah. We should be challenged whether there is with us any turning away from God’s word—what He is saying through His prophets.

I suppose Saul did not realise the seriousness of what he did. He was king, and I suppose he assumed that he need not obey anyone, but he was told that “rebellion is as the sin of divination”; that is, it is equally serious to that; it is equivalent. We should have a judgment of divination. It would suggest a forceful way of seeking to find out, through devious means, what the mind of God is. Balaam sought enchantments rather than enquiring of God and paying attention to His word. That might be seen in the way the religious mind forces itself against what has come to us through God’s word, in the power of the Spirit; as Mr. Darby said, the notion of a clergyman is, dispensationally, the sin against the Holy Spirit. On that line of things the Spirit is shut out through the forcing of
the flesh. Saul forced himself and offered (1 Samuel 13: 12); he did not wait as he was told to do. Then he saved the best of the flesh.

These things are challenging to us, because they were written for our admonition—they happened as types of us. We want to get the gain of these scriptures and see that God is not having any self-will or rebellion; He will take issue with it, as He did here.

Although Samuel is speaking in power here, the chapter finishes with him unduly mourning for Saul. And we might say what is right and not really be up to what we say. God would challenge us, because He said to Samuel, “How long wilt thou mourn for Saul, seeing I have rejected him?”, 1 Samuel 16: 1. Once God acts, “the Hope of Israel will not lie nor repent; for he is not a man, that he should repent”, 1 Samuel 15: 29. There is no change with God once He decides something. In certain instances we are told that God repented, but that was in relation to a change with persons. God remains the Same; He does not change (Psalm 102: 27). Therefore we should be exercised that we have the same view of things as God. If His view is different from ours, we should get adjusted at once.

God would awaken us; He would stir up His prophets; He would have them active. He used Samuel here, and He continues to use the prophets to stir us up. We should be concerned to have the prophetic word made surer, for God is not giving up His great thoughts, but is rising up early and sending His prophets, as it says in Jeremiah 7: 2. He told Samuel to go and anoint a king among the sons of Jesse. God had His king! Samuel has to say, concerning Jesse’s sons that were present, “Jehovah has not chosen these”, 1 Samuel 16: 10. He

had needed adjustment to discern that none of them was the man of God’s choice. It took time; when he saw Eliab, the first, he said, “Surely Jehovah’s anointed is before him”. But he got adjusted, and, said as to all those present that Jehovah had not chosen them. It is truly wonderful to get adjusted, not only outwardly, but inwardly, as to the line of things with which God is proceeding. We want to be in accord with the way God sees things. He would tell us, through the prophetic word, that “obedience is better than sacrifice, Attention than the fat of rams”.

How much there is in the way of outward worship and religiousness in christendom, but with little attention given to what is coming out prophetically. God would have us to be in the current of the prophetic line of things today. The word of God is living and operative; not a dead order of things. We have come here this evening to get what is prophetic, and to be stirred up by it; to be challenged, and to be conscious that God is amongst us. We are, so to speak, brought to attention as to where we are and who God is, and where He would have us. Saul wanted Samuel to turn again after him and honour him, but we must see that God has set aside the flesh completely. He is not having that; He is not going to change His mind about that, and He would have us in accord with His thoughts about it.

As I said, I was challenged by our brother’s prayer that self-will might not interfere with the word. It may do so, in the sense that we might elect not to speak, for example, or it might interfere in the sense that we push ourselves forward, not having a word from God. Thus we would be challenged as having to do with the living God. There is what He has prescribed, even as to a meeting such as this, and He wants us to pay attention to

His word; to be obedient and not on the line of divination, which would be using the natural mind to conjecture how it might be this way or that way. So let us be on the line of inquiry and attention to what God would say to us prophetically.

articles.title: AUTHORITY
articles.author: J. E. Mutton
articles.meeting: Substance of word in meeting for ministry

paragraphs.text: It is interesting to note that a little later in this chapter we get the expression “Behold your king” (John 19: 14). What a contrast to what our brother has spoken of in Zechariah 9: 9 and Psalm 24: 7–10, “Behold, thy King cometh”—in majesty. But here He is coming forth as rejected, wearing the crown of thorn and the purple robe. It is the same King, the same Jesus, meekly accepting the reproaches of men. “Behold your king” was said in derision, yet how it appeals to our hearts!

What I have in mind is the distinctiveness of authority, and where it is found. First of all, it is absolute in God Himself (1 Timothy 6: 15). There should be no challenging of this, for God is God. But He has the prerogative to delegate authority to others. This tests us, but is for our salvation. There is no authority except what is given from above. Earlier in this gospel the Lord speaks of Himself as “from above”, “He who comes from above is above all”, John 3: 31. He also presents Himself as having been given authority to execute judgment
because He is Son of man (John 5: 27). He had taken His place in manhood.

Man as a creature was placed in authority over the animals—he named them all. The theory of evolution is rubbish; man was created and placed in dominion. The history of man has been a history of failure, yet all that man has lost is established in Christ “crowned ... with glory and honour” and “set ... over the works of thy hands”, Hebrews 2: 7.

Then man, as under Christ, is placed in authority over woman, and the woman is to recognise this, having on her head ‘a token of the authority under which she stands’, “on account of the angels”, 1 Corinthians 11: 10 (and see footnote in N.T.). I feel grieved to notice at times the absence of the token, for it is a part of Paul’s ministry. His ministry has authority. He tells us it was authority given to him by the Lord for building up and not for overthrowing (2 Corinthians 10: 8; 13: 10). Ministry is to be positive, “for building up”. Paul says, “He that prophesies edifies the assembly”, 1 Corinthians 14: 4. What need there is for this, and, thank God, it remains in our day.

Paul wrote to Corinth recognising the assembly there, and the delegated authority from above that it had been given in respect of its own matters. He had learnt this at his conversion when he asked, “What shall I do, Lord?”. The Lord did not give a direct answer but said, “Rise up and enter into the city, and it shall be told thee what thou must do”, Acts 9: 6. God had given authority from above to the disciples in that city. Each local assembly has authority within its own boundary—but “no authority whatever” elsewhere. Various crises in the history of the recovery have involved this principle. We have to go back only some four years
to recall such an issue, emphasizing the need to recognise the authority given to a local assembly to act in its own area.

But we are not to live on conflict. What follows a crisis is to be a fresh forward movement. When Israel came to the Red Sea the word was, “Speak into the children of Israel, that they go forward”, Exodus 14: 15. This was the word of authority given from above in the ministry, and we must recognise authority in ministry. He has “given to his bondmen the authority, and to each one his work”, Mark 13: 34. We all have work to do for the Lord, and the bondman is given the authority. Moses was a bondman of Jehovah (Exodus 14: 31), so were Paul and John and others, and they so describe themselves. A bondman recognises the absolute authority over him—supreme authority in God Himself—and also what has been given to him to do. It also says that God reveals His secrets to His servants the prophets before He acts (Amos 3: 7). He has respect to His bondmen.

We need to recognise the authority given from above, for there has always been Satan’s attack through usurped authority. We have proved this in the past, as it says, “Other lords ... have had dominion over us” (Isaiah 26: 13), but this was not authority from above. Ministry can still be judged by, “Was it of heaven, or of men?”, Mark 11: 30.

Naturally, man resents authority in others, or tends to usurp it. Not only do we see this in world affairs, but we have seen it in the assembly. Our salvation lies in the recognition of authority given from above in the various settings in which God has been pleased to place it.

The Lord as coming into His garden (Song of Songs 5: 1) appreciates what is there for Him— so it is His myrrh, His honeycomb, and so on. We should each be able to bring myrrh, as did the woman in Luke 7, having an appreciation of His suffering love. The honeycomb would be the product of the activity of many, so we afford something for the Lord together which we could never provide alone. The appreciation of the inheritance suggested in the wine and milk would be for Him. Then we are His friends and He bids us eat, that is, to feed on Himself who was entirely devoted here to the will of God. This is truly food and it is expressed in the Supper. To “drink, yea, drink abundantly” suggests the wonderful wealth of divine love and favour into which we have been brought, the new covenant of which He is the Mediator. So we are His beloved ones—kindred to Him, His assembly and His confidantes. He would have us drink deeply into the fulness of divine love.
Kingston, Ont.
“The man Christ Jesus”—1 Timothy 2: 5
I wake in the morning with thoughts of His love,
Who is living for me in the glory above,
Ev’ry minute expecting He’ll call me away,
And that keeps me bright all the rest of the day!
But the moments speed forward, and on comes the noon,
Yet still I am singing, ‘He’ll come very soon’,
And thus I am watching from morning till night,
And pluming my wings to be ready for flight!
There’s a Man in the glory I know very well,
I have known Him for years, and His goodness can tell,
One day in His mercy He knocked at my door,
And, seeking admission, knocked many times o’er.
But when I went to Him and stood face to face,
And listened awhile to His story of grace,
How He suffered for sinners, and put away sin,
I heartily, thankfully welcomed Him in.
We have lived on together a number of years,
And that’s why I neither have doubtings nor fears,
For my sins are all hid in the depths of the sea,
They were carried down there by the Man on the tree.
I am often surprised why the lip should be curled,
When I speak of my Lord to the man of the world,
And notice with sorrow his look of disdain,
When I tell him that Jesus is coming again.
He seems so content with his houses and gold,
While despising the ark, like the people of old;
And yet at His coming I’m sure he would flee,
Like the man in the garden, who ate of the tree.
I cannot but think it is foolish of souls
To put all their money ‘in bags which have holes’,
To find in the day that is coming apace,
How lightly they valued the ‘riches of grace’.
And fond as I am of His work in the field,
I would leave go the plough, I would lay down the shield—
The weapons of service I would put on the shelf,
And the sword in its scabbard, to be with Himself.
But I’ll work on with pleasure, while keeping my eyes
On the end of the field where standeth the prize,
I would work for His glory, that when we shall meet,
I may have a large sheaf to lay down at His feet.
That He, too, with pleasure His fruit may review—
Is the Man in the glory a stranger to you?
A stranger to Jesus! What, do you not know,
He is washing poor sinners much whiter than snow?
Have you lived in a land where the Bible’s unknown,
That you don’t know the Man who is now on the throne?
Ah, did you but know half His beauty and power,
You would not be a stranger another half-hour.
I have known Him so long that I’m able to say,
The very worst sinner He’ll not turn away.
The question of sin I adoringly see,
The Man in the glory has settled for me!
And as to my footsteps, whatever the scene,
The Man in the glory is keeping me clean;
And therefore I’m singing, from morning till night,
The Man in the glory is all my delight.

SPIRITUAL PANORAMAS It always adds to the interest of a view when, at the summit of a high hill or mountain, there is an indicator identifying points perhaps as far as fifty miles away in all directions. There are also spiritual panoramas, and Moses had a keen appreciation of them. His acute vision would have enabled him to discern far-distant objects.

From the top of Pisgah he would have looked “over the surface of the waste” (Numbers 21: 20)—and it is a healthy thing for us to look back and trace the way in which divine mercy and grace have faithfully led and preserved us. But from the same summit, just before he died, Moses was shown by Jehovah “the whole land” which had been promised to the patriarchs (Deuteronomy 31: 1–4). How fine a prospect to look out over the vast range of the inheritance, the things which God has prepared for them that love Him, involving every spiritual blessing. The great scope of Moses’ vision is seen in Psalm 90 as he declares worshipfully, “Even from eternity to eternity thou art God”. But Moses’ finest view was granted to him when, on “a high mountain apart” (Matthew 17: 1), he was found in holy converse with Jesus and beheld the glory of Him who, through His operations in time, has brought into fruition all the purposes of eternity, and sustains all, now and eternally for divine pleasure. It is in the service of God that we get the most glorious glimpses of the grand scope of divine purposes and operations, and of God’s delight and rest in their eternal results.

POWER TO DEAL WITH EVIL Near the Cornish coast we were arrested by the cries of seagulls overhead. Looking up, we saw a flock of gulls and, in the middle of them, the menacing shape of a buzzard. There was no fighting; it seemed as if the bird of prey was being irresistibly moved on. As the gulls acted together in the instincts of self-preservation, it just had to retreat. This left a strong impression of the power the christian has, by the Holy Spirit, to expel from his mind sinful suggestions and thoughts. It also illustrates the way in which believers, set together in the light of the assembly, have power to act should there be any intrusion of

evil in teaching or conduct. How pleasing it is to the Lord to see His people acting as one man so that evil is named, judged, and repudiated, though the desire would be that the persons involved in it might be saved.

The work of God for us at the cross; the work of God in us by His the ways of God with us down here, are the activities of His love in order to bring us into the light of His purpose for us, where restful love is known. So that we can say amid the changing scenes of this life, “But we do know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to purpose”, Romans 8: 28. “My heart is fixed, O God”, Psalm 108: 1
Wm. Johnson (‘Quiet Resting Places’, p.8)

Time is precious and it is for us to fill it out, not only in regard to our personal history but the history of the assembly; the little that remains is to be redeemed and used for the Lord and naught else.
